SubTopics: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators `10or100`.
Content: Which fraction is equal to `0.53`?

Key.Rationale: This choice uses `53` as the denominator of a unit fraction rather than as the numerator of a `text(hundredths)` fraction.
This choice recognizes that `0.53` represents `53` `text(hundredths)` and writes this as a fraction with `53` in the numerator and `100` in the denominator.
This choice recognizes that `0.53` represents `53` `text(hundredths)` but inverts the fraction.

This choice recognizes that `53` should be in the numerator but uses `10` in the denominator based on either `10and53` both being `text(two-digit)` numbers OR the `text(first nonzero)` digit being in the `text(tenths)` place.

SubTopics: Read and write whole numbers in expanded, standard, and word form through `1text(,)000text(,)000`.
Content: The depth of the deepest part of the ocean is `36text(,)070` `text(feet)`. What is the depth, in `text(feet)`, of the deepest part of the ocean written in word form?

Key.Rationale: This choice misreads the place value of the `7` as the `text(ones)` place rather than the `text(tens)` place.

This choice recognizes that the `36` is in the `text(thousands)` period, reading this period as “`text(thirty-six thousand)`,” and then recognizes that `070` is `70`, reading this period as “`text(seventy)`”.
This choice omits the last (rightmost) `0` and reads the place values of the digits as though the number were `3text(,)607`.
This choice omits the `text(first)` (leftmost) `0` and reads the place values of the digits as though the number were `3text(,)670`.

SubTopics: Round multi-digit whole numbers (through `1text(,)000text(,)000`) to any place.
Content: The areas, in acres, of Arches National Park and Great Basin National Park round to the same `text(thousand)` and the same `text(ten thousand)`. The area of Arches National Park is `76text(,)519` acres. Which value could be the area, in `text(acres)`, of Great Basin National Park?

Key.Rationale: This choice selects the `text(first)` number that has the same digit in the `text(ten-thousands)` place `(7)` as `76text(,)519` but does not consider that `72text(,)658` rounds to `73text(,)000` `(text(thousand))` and to `70text(,)000` `(text(ten thousand))` whereas `76text(,)519` rounds to `77text(,)000` `(text(thousand))` and to `80text(,)000` `(text(ten thousand))`.

This choice selects a number that has the same `text(thousands)` period `(76text(,)000)` as `76text(,)519` but does not consider that, when rounding to the `text(thousand)`, `76text(,)419` rounds down to `76text(,)000` because of the `4` in the `text(hundreds)` place whereas `76text(,)519` rounds up to `77text(,)000` because of the `5` in the `text(hundreds)` place.

This choice starts with `76text(,)519`, rounding this to `77text(,)000` `(text(thousand))` because of the `5` in the `text(hundreds)` place and to `80text(,)000` `(text(ten thousand))` because of the `6` in the `text(thousands)` place, and then identifies that `77text(,)100` also rounds to `77text(,)000` `(text(thousand))` because of the `1` in the `text(hundreds)` place and to `80text(,)000` `(text(ten thousand))` because of the `7` in the `text(thousands)` place.

This choice rounds `76text(,)519` to the `text(ten thousand)`, resulting in `80text(,)000` because of the `6` in the `text(thousands)` place, and then identifies a number with `80` in the `text(thousands)` period without considering that, when rounding to the `text(thousand)`, `80text(,)933` rounds to `81text(,)000` whereas `76text(,)519` rounds to `77text(,)000`.

SubTopics: Use place-value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
Content: A student correctly divides a `text(four-digit)` number by `5`. The quotient has a remainder of `2`. Which number could be the digit in the `text(ones)` place of the dividend?

Key.Rationale: This choice determines the `text(ones)` place when multiplying `5` by a number with a `2` in the `text(ones)` place.
This choice subtracts `2` from an `text(odd)` multiple of `5`.

This choice recognizes that every number that is divisible by `5` has either a `0` or a `5` in the `text(ones)` place and concludes that, by adding `2` to each of these digits, any number with a `2` `(0+2=2)` or a 7 `(5+2=7)` in the `text(ones)` place would have a remainder of `2` when divided by `5`.
This choice subtracts `2` from an `text(even)` multiple of `5`.

SubTopics: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number and multiply `2` `text(two-digit)` numbers.
Content: An office building has `32` floors. There are `98` light bulbs on each floor. The price to replace each light bulb is `$2`. What is the total price to replace all the light bulbs in the office building?

Key.Rationale: This choice does not regroup when multiplying `32` by `98`, resulting in an incorrect product of `3text(,)126`, and also does not regroup when multiplying `3text(,)126` by `2`.
This choice does not regroup when multiplying `32` by `98`, resulting in an incorrect product of `3text(,)126`, but then correctly multiplies `3text(,)126` by `2`.
This choice multiplies `98` by `32`, resulting in a product of `3text(,)136`, but does not regroup when multiplying `3text(,)136` by `2`.

This choice multiplies `98` by `32`, resulting in a product of `3text(,)136` light bulbs, and then multiplies the number of light bulbs `(3text(,)136)` by `$2`, resulting in a product of `$6text(,)272`.

SubTopics: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100`) using the symbols `>,=,or<` and justify the conclusions.
Content: Carrie and D'Marco are reading copies of the same book. Carrie has read `3/10` of the book. D'Marco has read `2/3` of the book. Which sentence about the fractions of the book they have each read is true?

Key.Rationale: This choice compares the denominators but does not consider the numerators.
This choice compares the numerators and denominators separately.

C.Choice: Because the numerator of `3/10` is equal to the denominator of `2/3`, `3/10=2/3`.

Key.Rationale: This choice considers the fractions to be equal since the fractions share a common digit.

D.Choice: Because `3/10` is less than `text(half)` the book and `2/3` is more than `text(half)` the book, `3/10<2/3`.

Key.Rationale: This choice using a benchmark of `1/2`, recognizes that `3/10` is less than `1/2` since `3` is less than `text(half)` of `10` (which is `5`), recognizes that `2/3` is more than `1/2` since `2` is more than `text(half)` of `3` (which is `3/2`), and concludes that `3/10<2/3` since `3/10<1/2<2/3` (i.e., `3/10<1/2and1/2<2/3`).

SubTopics: Multiply a whole number by a unit fraction (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100` and final answers do not need to be simplified or written as a mixed number).
Add and subtract fractions with a common denominator (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100`; answers do not need to be simplified; and no improper fractions as the final answer).
Content: Minh stretches for `1/12` `text(hour)`. She runs for `6` times as long as she stretches. Then she walks for `2` times as long as she stretches. What fraction of an `text(hour)` does Minh spend stretching, running, and walking?

Key.Rationale: This choice determines the time spent running `(6xx1/12=6/12)` and the time spent walking `(2xx1/12=2/12)` but then finds the sum of `6/12+2/12` without including the time spent stretching `(1/12)`.

This choice multiplies `6` by `1/12` by multiplying the whole number `(6)` by the numerator `(1)`, resulting in a product of `6/12` `text(hour)`, multiplies `2` by `1/12` by multiplying the whole number `(2)` by the numerator `(1)`, resulting in a product of `2/12` `text(hour)`, and then finds the sum of `1/12+6/12+2/12` by adding the numerators `(1+6+2=9)` and leaving the common denominator `(12)`.

This choice determines the time spent running by adding `6` to the numerator of `1/12`, determines the time spent walking by adding `2` to the numerator of `1/12`, and then finds the sum of `7/12+3/12` without including the time spent stretching `(1/12)`.

This choice determines the time spent running by adding `6` to the numerator of `1/12`, determines the time spent walking by adding `2` to the numerator of `1/12`, and then finds the sum of `1/12+7/12+3/12`.

SubTopics: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.
Content: Sofi and Evan are collecting `text(pennies)` for school. Sofi has collected `141` `text(pennies)`. She has collected `3` times as many `text(pennies)` as Evan has collected. How many `text(pennies)` has Evan collected?

Key.Rationale: This choice sets up the equation as `141=3xx?`, rewrites the equation as `141-:3=?`, and then divides `141` by `3`.
This choice subtracts `3` from `141`, which would mean Sofi has collected `3` more `text(pennies)` than Evan has collected.
This choice adds `3` to `141`, which would mean Evan has collected `3` more `text(pennies)` than Sofi has collected.
This choice multiplies `141` by `3`, which would mean Evan has collected `3` times as many `text(pennies)` as Sofi has collected.

SubTopics: Identify the missing symbol `(+,-,xx,div,=,<,and>)` that makes a number sentence true (single-digit divisor only).
Content: A number sentence is shown below, but a symbol is missing.
:ibox:`16xx4-:2square32`
Which symbol should be placed into the box to make the number sentence true?

Key.Rationale: This choice recognizes that a comparison symbol is needed to complete the number sentence and then simplifies the expression to the left of the square by first multiplying `16` by `4`, resulting in a product of `64`, and then divides the product by `2`, resulting in a quotient of `32`, which is equal to the value to the right of the square `(32)`.

This choice either compares `64` to `32` (i.e., does not consider the `-:2`) OR compares `2` to `32` and reverses the meaning of the inequality symbol (i.e., considers `>` to represent “less than” rather than “greater than”).
This choice compares `2` to `32` and does not consider the “`16xx4-:`”.

This choice either selects another operation but does not consider that the result is an expression and not a number sentence OR selects the operation that would make `16xx4` equal to `2square32` without considering that the middle symbol is division `(-:)` rather than equals `(=)`.

SubTopics: Develop and apply number theory concepts to represent numbers in various ways.
Content: Eric picked `36` apples at an orchard. He packed all the apples he picked by putting `9` apples into each of `4` bags. What is another way Eric could have packed all the apples he picked?

A.Choice: by putting `6` apples into each of `6` bags

Key.Rationale: This choice recognizes that `6xx6=36`.

B.Choice: by putting `8` apples into each of `4` bags

Key.Rationale: This choice confuses `8xx4and9xx4`.

C.Choice: by putting `11` apples into each of `2` bags

Key.Rationale: This choice adds `2` to the `9` apples and subtracts `2` from the `4` bags.

D.Choice: by putting `15` apples into each of `3` bags

Key.Rationale: This choice recognizes that `15xx2=30` but then considers `1` more bag would equal `36`.

Content: A number pattern starts with the number `7`. The pattern follows the rule “add `10`.” What digit is in the `text(ones)` place of the `text(twelfth)` number in the pattern?

Key.Rationale: This choice uses the digit in the `text(ones)` place of the rule “add `10`” (i.e., does not consider that the pattern starts with `7`).
This choice uses the digit in the `text(ones)` place of `12` (i.e., considers the `text(twelfth)` number of the pattern to be `12`).
This choice recognizes that repeatedly adding `10` to a number does not affect the digit in the `text(ones)` place.
This choice adds `12` to `7` (i.e., considers the `text(twelfth)` number of the pattern to be `12` more than `7`) and identifies the digit in the `text(ones)` place.

Content: In the picture shown below, the `text(two)` rectangles have the same length and the same width.

Line segment `bar(BE)` will be added to the picture to create additional figures. Which statement about figure `BEHC` and figure `BFGC` is true?

A.Choice: Both figure `BEHC` and figure `BFGC` will be rectangles.

Key.Rationale: This choice recognizes that angles `BCHandEHC` are right angles and determines that angles `CBEandBEH` will also be right angles, resulting in figures `BEHCandBFGC` both being rectangles since all `text(four)` angles in each figure are right angles.

B.Choice: Neither figure `BEHC` nor figure `BFGC` will be a rectangle.

Key.Rationale: This choice does not recognize that angles `CBEandBEH` will also be right angles.

C.Choice: Figure `BEHC` will be a rectangle, but figure `BFGC` will not be a rectangle.

Key.Rationale: This choice does not consider that `text(two)` rectangles sharing a side form a larger rectangle.

D.Choice: Figure `BEHC` will not be a rectangle, but figure `BFGC` will be a rectangle.

Key.Rationale: This choice does not consider that angle `BEH` will be a right angle.
